Guided Inquiry

The 1909 experiment

A collimated beam of α particles (helium nuclei, charge +2) strikes a thin gold foil. Geiger and Marsden could rotate a zinc-sulfide scintillation screen around the foil to count flashes at any angle θ.

Before you fire anything: think about the atom the way Thomson did in 1904 — a diffuse pudding of positive charge with electrons stuck in it, atom radius ≈ 100 pm. The α is fast (7.7 MeV) and heavy compared to the electrons.

Press Next → when you're ready to predict what happens.

Predict — what will the detector see?

You fire billions of α particles at the foil. In the plum-pudding picture, how are the scintillations distributed on the detector ring?

Observe — fire the beam

Press ▶ Play. Every α is counted, and every single one lands in the same spot: a bar at θ ≈ 0, within a few hundredths of a degree of straight through. The whole wide-angle arc stays dark, exactly as predicted.

Now switch Atomic model to Nuclear (Rutherford). The forward bin still dominates — but yellow now appears at 90° and beyond, and the counter shows that only about 1 α in 50 is deflected past 5° at all.

What does a wide-angle flash tell you?

Yellow now reaches past 90° — about 1 in 500 of the α particles that are counted, and roughly 1 in 25 000 of the whole beam. Some come almost straight back. What must be true about the target?

Bound the nucleus

One α is now fired head-on (b = 0). It climbs the Coulomb hill until all its kinetic energy has become potential energy, stops at the distance of closest approach , and is thrown back along its own path.

The α reaches that distance and still scatters as pure Coulomb — no contact, no nuclear force — so the nucleus must be smaller than . That is the payoff: an upper bound on the nuclear radius, read off a scattering experiment.

The full picture

Sweep Target Z: the counted rate scales as Z², so carbon barely registers while uranium floods the ring. Sweep α energy: the rate falls as 1/E², but the shape of the angular distribution does not move — sin−4(θ/2) has no energy in it. Every count comes from sampling the Rutherford cross section, so the shape is not drawn; it is measured by the running experiment.

You can now use the sim freely. Toggle ∑ Formal to see the equations behind the curve.

01

At a glance

An α source fires a narrow beam at a thin gold foil. A detector ring counts the flashes at each angle θ from the original direction. You can compare two pictures of the atom, then follow single α particles.

What you'll learn

  • How the angle θ depends on where an α is aimed.
  • What each model of the atom says the detector ring will count.
  • What a head-on α tells you about the target.
  • How the count depends on the target charge Z and the α energy.
The beam meets the foil. The detector can sit anywhere on the ring, and θ is measured from the beam's original direction.

What's on screen

  • Source, foil, ring: the dashed ring is marked in degrees.
  • Yellow flashes and bars: each flash is one α counted. Bar length follows the log of the counts in a 5° bin.
  • Single-shot view: an orange track past one nucleus, with a blue b line and a green θ arc.
  • Live readouts: d, θ, the counts and the counted fraction.
See itLook at the apparatus before anything is fired. Watch for: the α source, the foil strip, and the dashed ring marked from 0° to 180°.

03

In a plum-pudding atom an α is deflected by about 10⁻⁴ rad

Thomson's atom spreads the positive charge over the whole atom, with electrons stuck in it. The sim takes the atom's radius as Ratom = 1.35×10⁵ fm. An α is about 7300 times heavier than an electron, so electrons barely matter. What deflects the α is the positive charge, and spread out it pushes weakly:

θmax ∼ z1z2e² / (4πε0 Ek Ratom)
z₁ = 2 for the α and z₂ = Z for the target.

For gold and 7.7 MeV this is 2.19×10⁻⁴ rad, about 0.0125°. So every α should come out within a tiny forward cone, and the wide-angle arcs of the ring should stay dark.

See itChoose the plum pudding model, in Beam mode, and press Play. Watch for: every count in the forward bar, inside θ ≈ 0.025°, with wide-angle arcs stay dark on the ring.
04

A nucleus sends a few α far off course

Rutherford's atom packs all the positive charge into a tiny nucleus. The Coulomb force on an α goes as 1/r², so the path is a smooth hyperbola. The α never touches the nucleus. How far it turns depends on the aim b, the miss distance of its original line:

b = (d / 2) cot(θ / 2)
d = z1z2e² / (4πε0 Ek) = 29.55 fm for a 7.7 MeV α on gold.
b (fm)2001005020100
θ8.4°16.8°32.9°72.9°111.8°180°

A beam is spread over the foil, and few α pass close to a nucleus. About 1 in 47 turn by more than 5°. Of those, about 1 in 525 pass 90°, which is 1 in 25 000 of the whole beam.

See itChoose the nuclear model, in Beam mode, and press Play. Watch for: yellow bars reaching past 90°, and a counted fraction near 1 in 47.
See itUse Single shot with b = 50 fm. Watch for: the orange track bending away from the nucleus by θ = 32.9°.
05

A head-on α bounds the size of the nucleus

Fire an α straight at the nucleus, b = 0. It climbs the Coulomb hill, slowing down, until all its kinetic energy has become electric potential energy. There it stops for an instant, then goes back along its path. Setting Ek = z₁z₂e²/(4πε₀d) gives the closest approach d, the same d as in the last section.

At d the α is still scattered by the Coulomb force alone, with no sign of the nuclear force. So the nucleus must be smaller than d. For 7.7 MeV on gold that is 29.55 fm, an upper limit and not a measured size. Later experiments found gold's nuclear radius to be about 7 fm.

Ek (MeV)137.720
d on gold (fm)227.575.829.511.4

A faster α gets closer, so a higher energy gives a tighter bound.

See itUse Single shot with b = 0 on gold at 7.7 MeV. Watch for: the α turning back, θ = 180°, and the marker closest approach = 29.5 fm.
06

The counts follow sin⁻⁴(θ/2), Z² and 1/E²

Counting α in each angle gives Rutherford's formula for the differential cross section:

dσ/dΩ = ( z1z2e² / (16πε0Ek) )² / sin⁴(θ/2)
Energy and charge set the size. θ alone sets the shape.

It is 4300 times larger at 10° than at 90°, so the yellow bars use a log scale. Doubling the energy cuts the counted fraction by 4. A bigger Z raises it as Z². The sim keeps the sweep between 5° and 175°, because the formula blows up at θ = 0.

FoilEk (MeV)counted fraction
Z = 797.71 in 47
Z = 927.71 in 35
Z = 793.01 in 7
Z = 67.71 in 8 200
See itUse gold at 3.0 MeV in Beam mode and press Play. Watch for: a counted fraction near 1 in 7, many more than the 1 in 47 at 7.7 MeV.
07

Where it matters

  • The nuclear atom. This experiment replaced the plum pudding with a tiny, heavy, positive nucleus. Later models of the atom start from it.
  • Rutherford backscattering. Firing ions at a thin film and counting those that bounce back tells a lab what the film is made of and how thick it is.
  • Probing the nucleus. At energies high enough to reach the nucleus, the counts depart from Rutherford's formula, and the departure measures its size.
  • Radioactive sources. The α energies used here, a few MeV, are those of real α-emitting nuclei, so the same Coulomb arithmetic applies.
08

Summary

In one line. Counting how α particles scatter from a foil tells you how the atom's charge is arranged.

Key points

  • A plum-pudding atom turns an α by only about 10⁻⁴ rad. Large angles need a concentrated charge.
  • The path is a Coulomb hyperbola, with b = (d/2) cot(θ/2) and d = z₁z₂e²/(4πε₀Ek).
  • The head-on closest approach d is an upper bound on the nuclear radius.
  • The counts follow sin⁻⁴(θ/2), and the counted fraction goes as Z²/E².

Common mix-ups

  • "The α bounces off the nucleus like a billiard ball." The Coulomb force acts at a distance, and the path is a smooth hyperbola with no contact.
  • "d is the radius of the nucleus." It is the closest approach reached, so the nucleus is no bigger than that.
  • "A higher energy gives a different angular pattern." It changes how many α are counted, and the sin⁻⁴(θ/2) shape stays.

Things to try on your own

  • Find the b that gives θ = 90° at 7.7 MeV, and check it against d/2.
  • Compare the counted fraction of carbon and uranium.
